samples.summary: New CLI can never log in against a backend that does not echo `state` — contradicts the change's own back-compat claim and acceptance criterion
samples.evidence: `startCallbackServer` refuses every callback whose `state` does not equal the nonce (`if (!nonceMatches(expectedNonce, state)) { … res.writeHead(400); return; }`), and `settled` is only set by a matching callback. Against a server that ignores `nonce=` (no `&state=` on the loopback redirect) the promise is never resolved: the user waits the full 30s timeout (line 293) and then gets a hard failure. docs/design/cli.md:218 states "Both are optional on the wire, so a new CLI still works against a server that predates them", and docs/tasks/active/20260812-cli-login-loopback-binding-todo.md:68 lists as an acceptance criterion "`wafflebase login` still completes end to end against a backend that ignores both new parameters" — and marks it [x]. Neither holds. The same task doc (line 17-22) records that the previous attempt was reverted precisely because "a hard requirement on a `state` echo only the new backend sends (an older server turned every login into a silent 30-second timeout)"; this change reinstates that behaviour, changing only the wording of the eventual error. Either the code must degrade (e.g. accept a state-less callback when the flow can be shown to predate the echo, or fail fast) or the doc/AC is false.

samples.summary: Old-backend diagnosis only fires for a literally absent `state`, so the explanatory timeout message is missed for `state=`
samples.evidence: `if (state === null) sawUnboundCode = true;` — `url.searchParams.get('state')` returns `''` (not `null`) when the redirect carries `?state=` with an empty value, and `nonceMatches` rejects `''` via `if (!received) return false`. In that case `sawUnboundCode` stays false and the user gets the generic "Login timed out" message instead of the upgrade hint the branch exists to give. `if (!state)` would cover both.

samples.summary: `await failFromBackend(...)` does not terminate control flow for the type checker, so the failure paths fall through if the exit is ever prevented
samples.evidence: `if (!exchangeRes.ok) { await failFromBackend(exchangeRes, name, {…}); }` — TypeScript's never-returning-call narrowing applies to a bare call-expression statement, not to an `await` of a `Promise<never>`, so nothing marks lines 89+ unreachable. `failFromBackend` has already consumed the body (`await res.json()`), so any situation where `process.exit` does not actually terminate (a stubbed exit in tests, or a future refactor that returns instead of exiting) proceeds to `exchangeRes.json()` on a used body — a "Body is unusable" TypeError that masks the real failure — and for the `meRes`/`wsRes` cases would continue to `saveSession` with `undefined` fields. A `return`/`throw` at the call sites would make the termination explicit.

samples.summary: Download failure envelope can report a success status as the message
samples.evidence: The guard is `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes)`, but the fallback message passed to `backendErrorEnvelope` is `HTTP ${res.status}`. For the second arm (a 200 response that produced no bytes) the emitted envelope is `{"error":{"code":"HTTP_ERROR","message":"HTTP 200"}}`, which tells the caller the request succeeded while reporting a failure. A distinct code/message for the empty-body case would be correct.

samples.summary: `backendErrorEnvelope` silently drops every top-level body field except `message`, where the call sites previously printed the whole body
samples.evidence: The returned object is built only from `body.error`'s own fields plus the derived `code`/`message`. The converted call sites (docs.ts:202/268, notes.ts:155/216, slides.ts:161/218, docs/import.ts, notes/import.ts, slides/import.ts, files/upload.ts, files/download.ts) previously emitted `JSON.stringify(res.data, null, 2)` verbatim, so any diagnostic context a backend attaches at the top level (`statusCode`, `details`, field paths outside `message`) is now discarded from stderr. This is a behaviour reduction on the error path, not just a formatting change.

samples.summary: `runCli` registers a `preAction` hook on the program it is handed, accumulating one hook per invocation
samples.evidence: `program.hook('preAction', …)` runs on every `runCli` call, including calls that pass an existing `program` (the tests do). Repeated invocations with the same program attach duplicate hooks; harmless today because the hook only assigns `acting`, but it is state mutation of a caller-owned object.

samples.summary: `code_challenge` charset regex admits characters that can never appear in an S256 challenge
samples.evidence: `/^[A-Za-z0-9\-._~]+$/` allows `.` and `~`, which are not in the base64url alphabet the comment claims to enforce. A challenge containing them is accepted and stored, but `consumeCode`'s `createHash('sha256').digest('base64url')` can never equal it, so such a login is guaranteed to fail at exchange time with a generic "Invalid or expired code" instead of being rejected at ingestion.

finding.summary: New CLI can never log in against a backend that does not echo `state` — contradicts the change's own back-compat claim and acceptance criterion
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` refuses every callback whose `state` does not equal the nonce (`if (!nonceMatches(expectedNonce, state)) { … res.writeHead(400); return; }`), and `settled` is only set by a matching callback. verdict.reason: The code is present as described (login.ts:240-246 answers 400 and never resolves for a non-matching/absent `state`; only the timeout at line 293 ends the wait), so a new CLI against a server that ignores `nonce=` does wait 30s and then fail. However this is not a logic/runtime defect: it is the change's explicitly designed behavior. docs/design/cli.md:219-221 — the sentences directly after the line the reviewer quoted — state "When a code arrives with no `state` at all (which is what an older backend looks like), the CLI refuses it and the timeout message says so rather than reporting a bare timeout", and the task doc's own back-compat plan bullet (20260812-cli-login-loopback-binding-todo.md:41-45) says the state-less code "is still refused, but the timeout message names that cause". The implementation matches both, including the specific timeout message (login.ts:298-302) and the intentional decision to keep the listener open so a probe cannot abort a genuine login (login.ts:237-239). Refusing an unbound code is the RFC 8252 §8.9 injection binding; asking the CLI to accept a state-less callback is a security-design tradeoff this lens defers. In-repo the flow completes: the backend echoes the nonce (auth.controller.ts:127-131) and the CLI test drives the real login action to a successful exchange (login-callback.test.ts:147-162). No crash, data loss, dropped await, or swallowed error; the failure path emits an actionable message. What actually remains is that the acceptance-criterion line (todo:68-69) contradicts the same doc's plan bullet at 41-45, and cli.md:218's first sentence is loose before 219-221 qualifies it — a documentation-accuracy issue owned by a docs/design lens, not a Correctness-lens blocking defect.

finding.summary: Login callback server again redeems the first `code` that hits the loopback port, with no binding to the flow this process started
finding.evidence: This delta reverts the nonce/`state` echo end to end: `startCallbackServer()` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:153-182) now resolves `callbackPromise` for any `GET /callback?code=…` with no check that the code belongs to this login, `github-auth.guard.ts:24` no longer stores a nonce, and `auth.controller.ts:127` no longer echoes one back. The CLI then exchanges that code at `/auth/cli/exchange` and `saveSession()` (login.ts:138) persists whatever account it maps to, overwriting the user's session. The port is guessable and any page in the user's browser can navigate to it (RFC 8252 §8.9), so the terminal can be silently pointed at another account's session. The deleted `packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts` was the only regression guard. Primary ownership is the security lens; raised here because the outcome is a wrong/overwritten persisted session (state corruption), and because the delta also removes the only test of that behaviour.

verdict.reason: The described code state does not exist. The CLI callback server does bind the code to this flow: startCallbackServer(expectedNonce) (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:202) rejects with HTTP 400 'Invalid state' any /callback whose `state` does not constant-time-match the process nonce (login.ts:240-246, nonceMatches at login.ts:194-199); callbackResolve(code) is only reached past that gate (login.ts:287-290). The nonce and a PKCE code_challenge are minted and sent on the start URL (login.ts:45-56) and the verifier is sent at exchange (login.ts:79). The backend still stores the nonce (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:56-66) and still echoes it back as `state` on the loopback redirect (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:127-134). The test claimed deleted, packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts, is present and asserts 400 for missing/wrong/same-length-wrong state and 200+resolve for the matching state (lines 21-54), plus end-to-end nonce/PKCE wire-format coverage (lines 96-163). The finding's cited range login.ts:153-182 is the failFromBackend/ask helpers, not the callback handler. No other startCallbackServer implementation exists in the tree.
